title: Of first importance (1 Corinthians 15)
hookLine: Paul's summary, received and handed on: Christ died, was buried, was raised, appeared
tomorrow: how do you end a letter full of fights?

lines: ONE BOX. WHAT DO YOU KEEP?
cards: One box for a move. A phone with almost no storage left. Sooner or later everyone has to choose what to keep.
Paul makes that choice about faith near the end of this letter, and his answer fits in one breath. "For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received."
Received, then handed on, like something passed down a line of hands. So what made the cut?

teach.b: Four lines: "how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures: And that he was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve."
Appeared. Then Paul lists witnesses: "above five hundred brethren at once; of whom the greater part remain unto this present." Still around to be asked, he's saying.
Last of all, himself. Why spell it out?
Some in Corinth said there is no resurrection of the dead, and Paul won't soften it: "if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain." Now a neighbor.
In Acts, Paul calls himself a Pharisee, on trial "of the hope and resurrection of the dead."

teach.h: A HOPE PRAYED IN THE AMIDAH.
teach.b: That hope was Jewish before it was Christian, and it's still prayed. In the Amidah, a central Jewish prayer, one blessing praises God as the one who gives life to the dead.
Shared ground: a God who brings life out of death.
The honest difference: Paul says it has already begun, in one man.
"But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept." Jewish tradition doesn't see that beginning in Jesus, and keeps the hope ahead.
One hope, prayed in two houses, with a real difference about where it starts.

how: Christians proclaim Christ's death and resurrection in the creeds and at Easter; some churches read 1 Corinthians 15 at funerals.

games.q: you visit a friend's synagogue on Shabbat, and the prayer book praises God who gives life to the dead. your cousin whispers, 'wait, isn't that our line?' what's fair to say?
o: a hope both share; Christians say it began with Jesus, Jewish prayer doesn't.
it's exactly the same belief, so there's no difference worth naming.
they must have borrowed it from Christians, so it's really ours.
games.why: Paul the Pharisee spoke of the hope and resurrection of the dead; the Amidah still praises God who gives life to the dead. the difference: Paul says it began in Christ, the firstfruits.

practice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper, or whatever's nearest. Write four words, one per line: died, buried, raised, appeared.
Then read them back slowly, one breath each, letting each one land before the next, whether they're your words or, for now, simply Paul's.
